sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Observability is what separates code that runs in production from code that just runs. For Go engineers, this means knowing the three pillars—logs, metrics, traces—and their idiomatic Go implementations: slog for structured logging, prometheus/client_golang for metrics, and OpenTelemetry Go SDK for traces. Interviewers at production-focused companies ask about observability to gauge your operational maturity.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Three pillars, three questions: (1) Logs answer 'what happened?' — structured JSON logs with slog, log level severity, correlation via trace ID in log context. (2) Metrics answer 'how is the system behaving?' — Prometheus counters/histograms/gauges scraped by a Prometheus server. (3) Traces answer 'why is this request slow?' — OpenTelemetry spans propagated via W3C traceparent headers, exported to Jaeger or Tempo. In Go, instrument once at the transport/middleware layer so all handlers get automatic coverage.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Structured logging: key-value pairs, not printf strings; always include trace_id, user_id, and request_id fields. 2. log/slog (Go 1.21): slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil)), slog.InfoContext with attrs, handler chaining. 3. OpenTelemetry Go: otel.SetTracerProvider, tracer.Start(ctx, 'span-name'), span.SetAttributes, span.RecordError; propagator for HTTP headers. 4. Prometheus client: prometheus.NewCounterVec, prometheus.NewHistogramVec with buckets, promhttp.Handler() on /metrics endpoint, push vs. pull. 5. pprof: net/http/pprof, go tool pprof for CPU and memory profiles, continuous profiling with Pyroscope. 6. Scenario-based: how to debug a memory leak, a goroutine leak, and high p99 latency using the above tools.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you add structured logging to a Go HTTP service?' → slog with JSON handler, middleware to inject trace_id into context, log from context at handler level. • 'What Prometheus metric types would you use for HTTP request latency?' → Histogram with .Observe(duration.Seconds()) and appropriate buckets; use SummaryVec only when quantiles need to be accurate on the client. • 'How do you trace a slow request across three Go microservices?' → OpenTelemetry, trace propagation via HTTP header, visualise in Jaeger—look for the span with highest self-time. • 'How do you profile a Go service in production without restarting it?' → expose net/http/pprof on a non-public port, use go tool pprof -http: to visualise flame graph.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "My observability stack for a Go service has three layers. For logging I use log/slog with a JSON handler; all log calls go through slog.InfoContext so the trace ID from the request context is automatically included in every log line. For metrics I register a Prometheus histogram for HTTP request duration with pre-defined buckets matching our SLO (50 ms, 100 ms, 250 ms, 1 s) and expose a /metrics endpoint scraped by Prometheus. For traces I initialise the OpenTelemetry SDK in main with an OTLP exporter pointing at our Tempo collector, and I add a middleware that starts a root span for every HTTP request and propagates the traceparent header to all outbound calls. For production debugging I expose the pprof handlers on port 6060 inside the cluster—accessible via kubectl port-forward—so I can take CPU and heap profiles without a restart."
